newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel lays onus for recovery on Treasury.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel lays onus for recovery on Treasury.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel placed the onus of reviving Israel's slowing economy squarely on the Treasury at a news conference on Monday.

"They say when the economy is slowing it's not the time to keep to budget targets," Frenkel declared at a news conference to present the central bank's annual report. "I reject this completely. No budgetary restraint ever damages the economy."
His remarks followed hints by Treasury officials that Israel's slowing economy might require the government to exceed its target budget deficit of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product.
"I think at the present stage it would be a mistake to decide policies intentionally to miss targets," Frenkel said.

Frenkel said containing the budget was a key element "to make sure this slowdown remains shallow and brief." Finance Minister Dan Meridor is due to review spending after the first quarter, which ends on Monday.

"I take the government's statement that it means business," he said. "When it says it's going to try to reach its targets as far as the budget is concerned I take it seriously. Of course if we don't see that effort realised there will be room for concern because there will be basically two issues -- one, a loss of credibility and second, a loss for the economy."
Nevertheless, Frenkel said GDP would grow less than the officially projected 4.0 percent for 1997, which would mark a significant decline from 4.4 percent in 1996 and 7.1 percent in 1995.
"It will be below the four percent that was put into the budget, but it is too early to come up with a precise estimate," Frenkel said.
He rejected calls for an administrative devaluation and said the central bank had the resources to support the exchange rate.
"The Bank of Israel now sterilises through auctioning and bank deposits, and here we will just continue to do it as long as necessary," Frenkel said.

The Bank of Israel has been selling dollars almost daily in a bid to prevent the currency basket to which the Israeli shekel is officially linked from falling below the bottom end of its trading band. On Sunday, a Treasury official estimated that the Bank of Israel was spending some $300 million a day supporting the basket.

Recent strengthening of the dollar against European currencies has caused the basket rate to fall to the bottom of its trading band. However, although the shekel has weakened against the dollar it is still widely regarded as overvalued.

Over the last three years, the shekel's strength has been due to of wave of capital imports, as Israelis took out foreign currency loans to take advantage of lower overseas interest rates and foreigners invested heavily in the Israeli economy.

Frenkel said he saw indications that the shekel was beginning a period of a real depreciation, but warned that a major improvement in the exchange rate requires the government to take measures to keep the deficit in target.
"According to what research shows it appears we are beginning a process of a real depreciation," Frenkel said, citing reduced demand by Israelis for foreign currency loans.

"This of course will depend on implementing policies themselves .... It is critically important to keep on the matter of the budget deficit to the deficit reduction law and to the inflation target that the government set," he said.
Frenkel said the government should move forward with structural changes, especially in ending foreign currency controls.
"I would recommend that the government adopt as a strategic goal...to make the Israeli shekel fully convertible in world currency markets," he said.
He noted that with Israeli foreign currency reserves at record levels of nearly $14 billion, the government had the leeway to liberalise foreign exchange rules.
